hints: Think about what mitosis is for: does it make more chromosomes per cell, or share out identical copies? And what happens to the parent cytoplasm at cytokinesis?
Recall the end-replication problem in S phase: DNA polymerase cannot fully copy the very tip of the lagging strand, so what happens to telomere length every cycle?
walkthrough:
**Check chromosome number**

Think of mitosis as a careful sharing system. DNA is doubled in S phase, then sister chromatids are pulled apart equally.

Each daughter gets one full identical set, so chromosome number stays the same as the parent.

**Check volume of cytoplasm**

Now think about cytokinesis. One parent cell pinches into two daughter cells.

The parent cytoplasm is split roughly in half, so each new daughter starts smaller with a decreased volume. It will grow later in G1, but right after division it is smaller.

**Check length of telomeres**

This is the tricky one. Every time DNA replicates, a tiny bit of the telomere tip is lost because DNA polymerase needs a primer and works in one direction only.

This is called the end-replication problem, so telomeres get a little shorter with each cell cycle in most body cells.

**Put it together**

Remains the same for chromosomes, decreases for cytoplasm, decreases for telomeres.

That matches row D exactly.

options.A: Chromosome number does not increase in mitosis, it is kept constant. Cytoplasm is not the same, it is halved by cytokinesis.
options.B: Chromosome number does not increase, and telomeres do not stay the same length, they shorten due to the end-replication problem.
options.C: Chromosomes do stay the same, but cytoplasm and telomeres do not. Both decrease after one cycle.
options.D: Correct. Mitosis preserves chromosome number, cytokinesis halves cytoplasm volume, and DNA replication shortens telomeres.
